applicationInfo.name: Threat Model Export
applicationInfo.description: Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration for IoT workshop (AWS Workshop Studio / re:Invent builders session, also published as the public aws-samples/sample-aws-iot-pqc sample). ESP32-S3 field devices connect over MQTT/TLS 1.3 with a hybrid SecP256r1MLKEM768 key exchange to a containerized Mosquitto PQC broker (ECS Fargate in private subnets behind an internet-facing NLB on 8883 classical / 8884 ML-DSA-44), which bridges over classical mTLS to AWS IoT Core. Two Private CAs (classical ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-44) issue broker and device certificates. A cloud pipeline (API Gateway + Lambda registrar, CodeBuild firmware builder container, Step Functions PQC migration, S3 presigned-URL OTA) builds each firmware variant once (no device data in the image), issues each device's identity into a separate certs flash partition and migrates devices classical -> PQC key exchange -> PQC certificates over the air. An on-site Raspberry Pi (Builder-Pi, managed via SSM hybrid activation) runs a Flask GUI that registers and USB-flashes devices and hosts the 2.4GHz workshop WiFi AP. A CloudFront + S3 React dashboard backed by AppSync, Cognito, DynamoDB and IoT Rules -> Lambdas shows live telemetry and sends LED/OTA commands. Deployed per event from a single master CloudFormation stack in a throwaway account. In scope: device firmware, broker, NLB, PKI, build/registration/OTA/migration pipeline, Builder-Pi, dashboard and their AWS resources. Out of scope: AWS-managed service internals, the physical venue network beyond the workshop AP, attendee laptops.

assumptions.content: Each workshop runs in a throwaway AWS account (Workshop Studio per-event account, or pqc-a/pqc-b test accounts) that is torn down after the event.
The system holds no customer data, PII beyond optional dashboard identities, or regulated data; telemetry is synthetic device health data.
Attendees are semi-trusted: many are security practitioners with physical access to a board, the Builder-Pi station and the workshop WiFi.

Risk tolerance: a disrupted or visibly compromised live session at re:Invent is a reputational failure for a security workshop, so fleet-wide or cross-attendee attacks are not acceptable; single-device or workshop-scale availability issues are tolerable.
The public aws-samples repo is reference material; readers may reuse the design.
Operator Admin credentials are short-lived Isengard credentials obtained via ada, and upstream sources are pinned to release tags.

mitigations.content: Make every firmware variant refuse any OTA that does not carry a valid signature chained to the baked signer root (fail closed when sigAlg is missing), and have publish-ota sign every push including the classical era.

Verify the OTA download server: fix the wolfSSL chain issue (load the Amazon intermediate/roots and enable WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER with SNI and domain check) and only accept URLs whose host is the workshop firmware bucket's regional S3 endpoint.
Add a Mosquitto ACL that confines each device to its own topics: write dt/%u/#, read cmd/%u/#, using the certificate CN as the username (use_identity_as_username is already on).

Replace anonymous dashboard access: add a Cognito user pool (operator and per-event attendee sign-in), keep the unauthenticated role read-only, and allow mutations only to authenticated users scoped to their own device where possible.
Remove updateDevice from browser-callable access: only the telemetry processor writes device state, so scope the guest role's appsync:GraphQL to specific Query fields.
Throttle migrations: reject migrateFirmware while a device already has a migration in progress, cap start-migration concurrency, and set a CodeBuild concurrent-build limit.
Redact presigned URLs from logged OTA commands and shorten the presign expiry to the minimum the download needs.
Enable ESP32 flash encryption and secure boot v2 so device keys and the PSK cannot be read back over USB (production guidance; accepted for the workshop).
Make device identity revocable: enable CRLs on both Private CAs, revoke the device cert in the deregistrar, and have Mosquitto check the CRL (or an auth plugin that checks the registry).
Lock down the Builder-Pi GUI: require an operator token, add CSRF protection, make /api/config read-only at runtime, and bind the GUI away from the attendee AP interface.
Least-privilege Builder-Pi role: drop bucket-wide firmware read and registry Scan; the builder API returns a short-lived presigned URL for just the device being flashed.

Device identity is never in a firmware image: keys, certificates, CA roots and WiFi go into a separate certs NVS partition image built per device at registration, flashed by the Builder-Pi and then deleted from S3 (every version), with a 1-day lifecycle rule on identity/ as a backstop.

Keep the WiFi PSK only in SSM: the device-identity CodeBuild job reads it as a PARAMETER_STORE environment variable, and the registry, registrar, prepare-build and migration state machine no longer store or pass it.
Limit the SSM hybrid activation: registration limit of 1, expiry of hours not 7 days, and auto-deregister stale managed instances.
Enforce broker hostname checks on devices: add stable DNS names as SANs on both broker certificates and enable wolfSSL domain-name checking.

Harden the build supply chain: pin base images by digest, pin oqs-provider/OpenSSL commits and package versions, verify Arduino index signatures, use npm ci with a lockfile, and deploy images by digest with immutable ECR tags.
ECR scan on push for all three images.
Improve broker availability: run at least two broker tasks across AZs, set Mosquitto connection limits, and rely on Shield Standard on the NLB.
Make dashboard actions auditable: enable AppSync request logging and record caller identity once sign-in exists.
Narrow the bridge IoT policy to the device topic shapes (dt/esp32-*/telemetry, cmd/esp32-*/*) and remove the shadow wildcards it does not use.
Fail-closed public-mirror curation: publish-public-mirror.sh strips .kiro/ and .threatmodel/, scrubs account IDs, the PSK and internal URLs, and aborts if any survive.
Apply the same curation to the Workshop Studio source zip (package-workshop-src.sh), which currently ships .kiro/, .threatmodel/ and real account IDs.

Track the remaining classical-only links (IoT Core bridge TLS 1.2, OTA download, Builder-Pi HTTPS) and move them to hybrid ML-KEM where AWS endpoints support it; explain them in the workshop as the next migration step.
Mutual TLS required on both broker listeners, each trusting only its own Private CA, TLS 1.3 only.
Telemetry processor only updates devices that were registered (attribute_exists(serialNumber)), so unknown things cannot create dashboard cards.

Signed OTA verification when the command declares sigAlg: signer leaf must chain to the baked signer root (fails closed without a root), then the ECDSA-P256 or ML-DSA-44 signature must verify; signer keys are scrubbed from the build disk after signing.
Broker runs in private subnets with no public IP; its task role can read only the named broker and bridge secrets.
start-migration validates the requested variant against an allow-list before starting a migration.

Separate code signing from device identity: the OTA signer certificates are issued only by two dedicated firmware-signing root CAs (ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-44) with the codeSigning EKU; the device trusts only the signing root matching the image's sigAlg, requires codeSigning on the signer leaf, and never trusts a device CA root for OTA.

threats.prerequisites: with the identity pool ID from the public dashboard config.json
threats.threatAction: obtain Cognito guest credentials and call the AppSync migrateFirmware mutation for any thingName
threats.threatImpact: unrequested firmware builds and OTA pushes to any attendee's device, disrupting the live workshop and spending account resources
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with the identity pool ID from the public dashboard config.json can obtain Cognito guest credentials and call the AppSync migrateFirmware mutation for any thingName, which leads to unrequested firmware builds and OTA pushes to any attendee's device, disrupting the live workshop and spending account resources

threats.prerequisites: with Cognito guest credentials
threats.threatAction: call the AppSync updateDevice mutation to overwrite any device's firmwareVersion, pqcAlgorithm, tlsVersion or status
threats.threatImpact: a dashboard that shows false migration results, undermining the workshop's proof that devices negotiated ML-KEM
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with Cognito guest credentials can call the AppSync updateDevice mutation to overwrite any device's firmwareVersion, pqcAlgorithm, tlsVersion or status, which leads to a dashboard that shows false migration results, undermining the workshop's proof that devices negotiated ML-KEM

threats.prerequisites: with Cognito guest credentials within 15 minutes of a migration
threats.threatAction: read OTA commands through getDeviceLog and use a still-valid presigned URL to download the firmware image it points to
threats.threatImpact: access to the shared, identity-free firmware image only (the same code as the public repository), not to any device key or the WiFi PSK
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with Cognito guest credentials within 15 minutes of a migration can read OTA commands through getDeviceLog and use a still-valid presigned URL to download the firmware image it points to, which leads to access to the shared, identity-free firmware image only (the same code as the public repository), not to any device key or the WiFi PSK

threats.prerequisites: with Cognito guest credentials
threats.threatAction: read broker connection logs and all device message payloads through getBrokerLog and getDeviceLog
threats.threatImpact: disclosure of device client IDs, source IP addresses and full telemetry and command history
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with Cognito guest credentials can read broker connection logs and all device message payloads through getBrokerLog and getDeviceLog, which leads to disclosure of device client IDs, source IP addresses and full telemetry and command history

threats.prerequisites: with physical access to their own ESP32 board
threats.threatAction: dump the board's flash over USB and read the unencrypted certs NVS partition
threats.threatImpact: the attendee holding that board's two broker-trusted device identities (ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-44 keys and certificates) and the WiFi PSK, enabling the broker-level attacks
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with physical access to their own ESP32 board can dump the board's flash over USB and read the unencrypted certs NVS partition, which leads to the attendee holding that board's two broker-trusted device identities (ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-44 keys and certificates) and the WiFi PSK, enabling the broker-level attacks

threats.prerequisites: with a device certificate extracted from their own board
threats.threatAction: publish an ota-update with no sigAlg, a URL to their own HTTPS server and a matching sha256 to another device's cmd/<thing>/ota
threats.threatImpact: any device variant installing attacker-chosen firmware, because devices skip signature checks when sigAlg is absent and do not verify the download server's TLS certificate
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with a device certificate extracted from their own board can publish an ota-update with no sigAlg, a URL to their own HTTPS server and a matching sha256 to another device's cmd/<thing>/ota, which leads to any device variant installing attacker-chosen firmware, because devices skip signature checks when sigAlg is absent and do not verify the download server's TLS certificate

threats.prerequisites: with a device certificate extracted from their own board
threats.threatAction: publish dt/<other-thing>/telemetry or lifecycle messages for devices they do not own
threats.threatImpact: fake telemetry and PQC status for other attendees' devices on the dashboard and in the message log
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with a device certificate extracted from their own board can publish dt/<other-thing>/telemetry or lifecycle messages for devices they do not own, which leads to fake telemetry and PQC status for other attendees' devices on the dashboard and in the message log

threats.prerequisites: who obtained a device private key
threats.threatAction: reuse a deregistered or stolen device certificate to keep connecting to the broker indefinitely
threats.threatImpact: removed devices staying trusted, because the broker trusts any CA-issued cert, does not check the registry, and both CAs have CRLs disabled
threats.statement: A attacker who obtained a device private key can reuse a deregistered or stolen device certificate to keep connecting to the broker indefinitely, which leads to removed devices staying trusted, because the broker trusts any CA-issued cert, does not check the registry, and both CAs have CRLs disabled

threats.prerequisites: with the shared PSK
threats.threatAction: drive the unauthenticated Builder-Pi GUI to deregister or reflash other attendees' devices and read their serial consoles
threats.threatImpact: disruption of other attendees' devices and exposure of serial output
threats.statement: A user on the workshop WiFi with the shared PSK can drive the unauthenticated Builder-Pi GUI to deregister or reflash other attendees' devices and read their serial consoles, which leads to disruption of other attendees' devices and exposure of serial output

threats.prerequisites: with the shared PSK
threats.threatAction: POST to the Builder-Pi /api/config to re-point the firmware bucket or API endpoint to attacker-controlled resources
threats.threatImpact: the Pi flashing attacker-supplied firmware onto the next boards plugged into the station
threats.statement: A user on the workshop WiFi with the shared PSK can POST to the Builder-Pi /api/config to re-point the firmware bucket or API endpoint to attacker-controlled resources, which leads to the Pi flashing attacker-supplied firmware onto the next boards plugged into the station

threats.prerequisites: with root on the Builder-Pi or its role credentials
threats.threatAction: use the Pi role (bucket-wide s3:GetObject and the builder API) to read identity images that are waiting to be flashed, or register a serial to have a new identity issued
threats.threatImpact: disclosure of the keys of devices being registered and the ability to obtain broker-trusted device identities; firmware images carry no keys, and identity images exist in S3 only until flashed
threats.statement: A attacker with root on the Builder-Pi or its role credentials can use the Pi role (bucket-wide s3:GetObject and the builder API) to read identity images that are waiting to be flashed, or register a serial to have a new identity issued, which leads to disclosure of the keys of devices being registered and the ability to obtain broker-trusted device identities; firmware images carry no keys, and identity images exist in S3 only until flashed

threats.prerequisites: with a leaked Builder-Pi bundle within its 7-day validity
threats.threatAction: register their own machine with the hybrid activation code
threats.threatImpact: a rogue managed instance holding the Builder-Pi role, with the same bucket, registry and PSK access as the real Pi
threats.statement: A attacker with a leaked Builder-Pi bundle within its 7-day validity can register their own machine with the hybrid activation code, which leads to a rogue managed instance holding the Builder-Pi role, with the same bucket, registry and PSK access as the real Pi

threats.threatSource: user or role with read-only account access
threats.prerequisites: with CodeBuild, Step Functions or DynamoDB read permissions
threats.threatAction: read the workshop WiFi PSK from the CodeBuild project environment, build details, Step Functions execution history or the registry table
threats.threatImpact: disclosure of the PSK outside its SecureString
threats.statement: A user or role with read-only account access with CodeBuild, Step Functions or DynamoDB read permissions can read the workshop WiFi PSK from the CodeBuild project environment, build details, Step Functions execution history or the registry table, which leads to disclosure of the PSK outside its SecureString

threats.prerequisites: with the extracted PSK and network position in the room
threats.threatAction: run a rogue AP with the workshop SSID and PSK and present any certificate chaining to the workshop CA
threats.threatImpact: a man-in-the-middle on devices that associate with it, because the firmware checks the chain but not the broker hostname or SAN
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with the extracted PSK and network position in the room can run a rogue AP with the workshop SSID and PSK and present any certificate chaining to the workshop CA, which leads to a man-in-the-middle on devices that associate with it, because the firmware checks the chain but not the broker hostname or SAN

threats.prerequisites: such as the Ubuntu apt mirror, oqs-provider source, Arduino ESP32 core or npm registry
threats.threatAction: inject code into the broker, cert-issuer or firmware-builder image builds
threats.threatImpact: theft of the OTA signer keys and abuse of CA issuance, so malicious firmware can be signed for the whole fleet
threats.statement: A compromised upstream package source such as the Ubuntu apt mirror, oqs-provider source, Arduino ESP32 core or npm registry can inject code into the broker, cert-issuer or firmware-builder image builds, which leads to theft of the OTA signer keys and abuse of CA issuance, so malicious firmware can be signed for the whole fleet

threats.prerequisites: with ECR push permissions
threats.threatAction: push a replacement image under the mutable :latest tag in ECR
threats.threatImpact: Fargate and CodeBuild silently running attacker code with broker secrets or signer-key access on the next start
threats.statement: A insider or compromised principal with ECR push permissions can push a replacement image under the mutable :latest tag in ECR, which leads to Fargate and CodeBuild silently running attacker code with broker secrets or signer-key access on the next start

threats.prerequisites: with Cognito guest credentials
threats.threatAction: repeatedly call migrateFirmware across many devices
threats.threatImpact: queued or throttled CodeBuild builds that stall real migrations during the session, plus avoidable build cost
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with Cognito guest credentials can repeatedly call migrateFirmware across many devices, which leads to queued or throttled CodeBuild builds that stall real migrations during the session, plus avoidable build cost

threats.prerequisites: with modest bandwidth
threats.threatAction: flood the NLB on 8883/8884 with TLS handshakes
threats.threatImpact: exhaustion of the single Fargate broker task, disconnecting every device
threats.statement: A internet attacker with modest bandwidth can flood the NLB on 8883/8884 with TLS handshakes, which leads to exhaustion of the single Fargate broker task, disconnecting every device

threats.prerequisites: with Cognito guest credentials
threats.threatAction: migrate or overwrite devices through AppSync
threats.threatImpact: actions that cannot be attributed to a person, because all callers share the unauthenticated role
threats.statement: A anonymous internet user with Cognito guest credentials can migrate or overwrite devices through AppSync, which leads to actions that cannot be attributed to a person, because all callers share the unauthenticated role

threats.prerequisites: who compromises the broker task, e.g. via a Mosquitto or oqs-provider flaw
threats.threatAction: publish to dt/* and $aws/things/*/shadow/* and receive cmd/* for every device through the bridge identity
threats.threatImpact: fleet-wide telemetry spoofing and command interception in IoT Core from one compromised component
threats.statement: A attacker who compromises the broker task, e.g. via a Mosquitto or oqs-provider flaw can publish to dt/* and $aws/things/*/shadow/* and receive cmd/* for every device through the bridge identity, which leads to fleet-wide telemetry spoofing and command interception in IoT Core from one compromised component

threats.prerequisites: with publish rights
threats.threatAction: publish real account IDs, the PSK, .kiro notes or the threat model to the public mirror or the Workshop Studio source zip
threats.threatImpact: public disclosure of internal details and an attack roadmap
threats.statement: A maintainer making a mistake with publish rights can publish real account IDs, the PSK, .kiro notes or the threat model to the public mirror or the Workshop Studio source zip, which leads to public disclosure of internal details and an attack roadmap

threats.prerequisites: with a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer
threats.threatAction: record and later decrypt the classical-only links: bridge TLS 1.2, Builder-Pi HTTPS and the OTA firmware download from S3
threats.threatImpact: future disclosure of telemetry and of firmware images, contrary to the workshop's PQC message
threats.statement: A harvest-now-decrypt-later adversary with a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer can record and later decrypt the classical-only links: bridge TLS 1.2, Builder-Pi HTTPS and the OTA firmware download from S3, which leads to future disclosure of telemetry and of firmware images, contrary to the workshop's PQC message

threats.prerequisites: with a rogue AP using the workshop SSID and extracted PSK
threats.threatAction: intercept a device's OTA download, which does not verify the server certificate, and serve or capture the image
threats.threatImpact: capture of firmware images, and installation of a modified image on any device sent an unsigned OTA
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with a rogue AP using the workshop SSID and extracted PSK can intercept a device's OTA download, which does not verify the server certificate, and serve or capture the image, which leads to capture of firmware images, and installation of a modified image on any device sent an unsigned OTA

threats.prerequisites: with a device private key extracted from their own board
threats.threatAction: sign a modified firmware image with that key and push it to other devices as a signed OTA, because the OTA signer and device certificates are issued by the same CAs with the same extended key usage and devices only check that the signer chains to one of those CA roots
threats.threatImpact: every device accepting attacker-chosen firmware as authentic
threats.statement: A workshop attendee with a device private key extracted from their own board can sign a modified firmware image with that key and push it to other devices as a signed OTA, because the OTA signer and device certificates are issued by the same CAs with the same extended key usage and devices only check that the signer chains to one of those CA roots, which leads to every device accepting attacker-chosen firmware as authentic
